LOWER LIMB__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: lower-limb clinical anatomy is dominated by three themes — a nerve wrapped around a bone (common fibular at the fibular neck), a fracture that starves its own bone (intracapsular neck of femur → avascular necrosis), and a fascial compartment that can strangle its contents. Learn the site → structure → deficit chain and most OSCE and written questions fall out of it.
Peripheral Nerve Injuries — The Master Table

Seven nerves account for nearly all lower-limb neurology. Learn this grid cold — the rest of the section expands each row.

The sciatic nerve splits above the knee. Its two components — the tibial and common fibular — separate at the apex of the popliteal fossa. A high sciatic lesion mimics a combined tibial + common fibular palsy, but the common fibular part is more often affected (it is more lateral and tethered), so even a “sciatic” injury frequently presents as a foot drop.
Foot Drop, Trendelenburg & the Diagnostic Gaits
👟 Foot drop — Common fibular nerve
  • Loss of dorsiflexion (deep fibular → anterior compartment) and eversion (superficial fibular → lateral compartment)
  • Nerve is subcutaneous at the neck of the fibula → vulnerable to fracture, tight plaster, crossed legs, prolonged squatting
  • Gait: high-stepping (steppage) with a foot-slap; the patient lifts the knee high to clear the toes
  • Sensory: dorsum of foot; deep fibular gives the 1st web space
🚶 Trendelenburg — Superior gluteal nerve
  • Weak gluteus medius & minimus can’t stabilise the pelvis when standing on that leg
  • The pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side — “the sound side sags”
  • The lesion is on the stance (weak) side; bilateral disease → a waddling gait
  • Also seen in hip OA, DDH, and after hip surgery
Deep vs superficial fibular — split the foot drop. A deep fibular lesion loses dorsiflexion (foot drop) + the 1st web space sensation but keeps eversion. A superficial fibular lesion loses eversion + most of the dorsum of the foot but keeps dorsiflexion. Only a common fibular lesion loses both.

Weber classification & the Ottawa rules. Ankle fractures are graded by the level of the fibular fracture relative to the tibiofibular syndesmosis: A = below (stable), B = at the level (variable), C = above (syndesmosis disrupted → unstable). The Ottawa rules decide who needs imaging: the ankle rules → X-ray for tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of either malleolus or inability to weight-bear (4 steps); the foot rules → X-ray for tenderness at the navicular or the base of the 5th metatarsal.
The Hip — Blood Supply, AVN & Dislocation
Femoral head blood supply
  • Chiefly the medial femoral circumflex artery (from profunda femoris) → retinacular vessels ascending the neck under the capsule
  • Lateral femoral circumflex contributes less; the artery of ligamentum teres is minor (mostly relevant in children)
  • An intracapsular neck-of-femur # tears the retinacular vessels → AVN & non-union
  • Displaced intracapsular # → hemiarthroplasty / THR; extracapsular → dynamic hip screw
Hip dislocation & the fractured hip
  • A fractured NOF leg lies shortened & externally rotated
  • Posterior dislocation (~90%) — dashboard injury: limb flexed, adducted, internally rotated & shortened; the sciatic nerve is at risk
  • Anterior dislocation — limb abducted & externally rotated
The Femoral Triangle & Vascular Access
Borders & contents (“NAVEL”)
  • Borders: inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial); floor = iliopsoas + pectineus
  • Contents lateral→medial: femoral Nerve · Artery · Vein · Empty space (femoral canal) · Lymphatics
  • The nerve lies outside the femoral sheath (which contains artery, vein & canal)
Clinical access & the femoral hernia
  • Femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point (midway ASIS → pubic symphysis) — site for arterial lines / angiography / ABGs
  • The femoral vein (medial to the pulse) is used for central access & blood sampling
  • Femoral hernia = through the femoral canal, below & lateral to the pubic tubercle (vs inguinal: above & medial); commoner in women, high strangulation risk
The Popliteal Fossa
Borders & contents
  • Diamond: biceps femoris (superolateral); semimembranosus/tendinosus (superomedial); the two gastrocnemius heads (inferior)
  • Contents deep → superficial: popliteal artery (deepest, on the floor) → popliteal vein → tibial nerve (most superficial)
  • The common fibular nerve runs along the lateral border (on biceps tendon) before winding round the fibular neck
Clinical
  • Because the artery is deepest, the popliteal pulse is hard to feel (flex the knee to relax the fascia)
  • Knee dislocation / posterior trauma → popliteal artery injury (tethered at the adductor hiatus & soleal arch) — a limb-threatening emergency
  • Popliteal aneurysm — the commonest peripheral aneurysm (often bilateral, associated with AAA); Baker’s cyst is a common swelling
Compartment Syndrome of the Leg

The leg has four osteofascial compartments; the anterior is the most commonly affected.

CompartmentNerveAction lost
AnteriorDeep fibularDorsiflexion & toe extension
LateralSuperficial fibularEversion
Superficial posteriorTibialPlantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus)
Deep posteriorTibialInversion & toe flexion
Acute compartment syndrome. Classically after a tibial fracture or crush/reperfusion. Rising pressure → ischaemia → the 6 Ps (Pain out of proportion & on passive stretch — the earliest sign; Paraesthesia; Pallor; Pulselessness [late]; Paralysis; Perishingly cold). It is a clinical diagnosis → emergency fasciotomy; do not wait for a lost pulse.
Veins — Varicose Veins & DVT
The saphenous veins
  • Great (long) saphenous vein — passes anterior to the medial malleolus (reliable venous cut-down site), up the medial leg & thigh to the saphenofemoral junction; used as a bypass / CABG graft
  • The saphenous nerve runs with it below the knee — at risk during stripping/harvesting
  • Small (short) saphenous vein — behind the lateral malleolus → popliteal vein; runs with the sural nerve
Varicose veins & DVT
  • Varicose veins — incompetent valves (esp. at the SFJ & perforators) → dilated tortuous superficial veins
  • DVT — Virchow’s triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability); usually calf veins; risk of pulmonary embolism
  • Perforating veins connect the superficial to the deep system (one-way valves)
The Knee — Ligaments & the Unhappy Triad
The four ligaments
  • ACL — prevents anterior draw of the tibia; tested by the anterior drawer / Lachman
  • PCL — prevents posterior draw; posterior drawer / sag sign
  • MCL — resists valgus; LCL — resists varus
The unhappy triad
  • A lateral blow to the planted knee tears three structures: ACL + MCL + medial meniscus
  • The medial meniscus is more often injured — it is firmly attached to the MCL
  • Presents with effusion, locking & instability
⭐ Exam Pearls
Common fibular nerve = the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb (fibular neck) → foot drop.
Intracapsular NOF fracture threatens the femoral-head blood supply (medial femoral circumflex) → AVN.
Trendelenburg: the pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak (stance-leg) gluteus medius — “sound side sags”.
Femoral triangle NAVEL (lateral→medial); the nerve is outside the femoral sheath; pulse at the mid-inguinal point.
Femoral hernia = below & lateral to the pubic tubercle; inguinal hernia = above & medial.
Popliteal artery is the deepest structure → weak pulse; at risk in knee dislocation.
Compartment syndrome is clinical — pain on passive stretch is the earliest sign; fasciotomy before the pulse disappears.
Unhappy triad = ACL + MCL + medial meniscus; give IM injections in the upper-outer quadrant to avoid the sciatic nerve.
LOWER LIMB__Osteology & Joints:
Why this matters: the lower limb is built for weight-bearing and stability, not the mobility of the upper limb — so its bones are heavier, its joints deeper, and its ligaments stronger. Learn the landmarks (every muscle and ligament hangs off one) and the joint design (a deep hip socket, a locking knee, an ankle mortise), and you can reason out the movements, the stability and the fractures.
The Skeleton — Overview
Pelvic girdle
  • Hip bone (os coxae) — ilium + ischium + pubis, fused at the acetabulum
  • Transfers body weight from the axial skeleton to the limb via the sacroiliac joint
Free limb
  • Thigh: femur (+ patella)
  • Leg: tibia (medial, weight-bearing) & fibula (lateral)
  • Foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges
The Hip Bone (Os Coxae)

Three bones fuse at the cup-shaped acetabulum: the ilium (superior), ischium (posteroinferior) and pubis (anteroinferior).

Key landmarks
  • Iliac crest → ends as ASIS (front) & PSIS (back); AIIS & PIIS below
  • Greater & lesser sciatic notches, separated by the ischial spine
  • Ischial tuberosity — the “sit bone” (hamstring origin)
  • Pubic tubercle & crest; superior & inferior pubic rami; the obturator foramen
Clinical
  • The ischial spine converts the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen via the sacrospinous ligament
  • The ASIS (inguinal ligament, sartorius) & iliac crest (bone marrow biopsy) are palpable landmarks
  • Pelvic fractures risk major haemorrhage & bladder/urethral injury
Femur
RegionLandmarks
ProximalHead (with the fovea for ligamentum teres), neck, greater & lesser trochanters, intertrochanteric line (front) & crest (back)
ShaftLinea aspera (posterior ridge — adductor/vasti attachments), gluteal tuberosity, pectineal line
DistalMedial & lateral condyles & epicondyles, adductor tubercle, patellar surface, intercondylar fossa
The neck–shaft angle. Normally ~125°, angling the shaft medially so the knees sit under the body’s centre of gravity. Coxa vara (<120°) and coxa valga (>135°) alter gait and load. The femoral neck is also anteverted ~15°.
Patella, Tibia & Fibula
Patella & tibia
  • Patella — the largest sesamoid bone (in the quadriceps tendon); it improves the quadriceps lever arm
  • Tibia — the weight-bearing bone: medial & lateral condyles, intercondylar eminence, tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament), sharp anterior border (shin), soleal line, medial malleolus
Fibula
  • Head, neck (common fibular nerve winds here), shaft, lateral malleolus
  • Not weight-bearing — it is for muscle attachment, the lateral malleolus & the ankle mortise; can be harvested as a bone graft
Bones of the Foot

Seven tarsals, five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges. Learn the tarsals with “Tiger Cubs Need MILC” — Talus, Calcaneus, Navicular, and the Cuboid + Medial/Intermediate/Lateral cuneiforms.

Talus — transmits body weight to the foot; has no muscle attachments; its blood supply is retrograde → # risks AVN.
Calcaneus — the largest tarsal (heel); the sustentaculum tali supports the talus; Achilles tendon inserts here.
Navicular — keystone-adjacent on the medial side; tuberosity for tibialis posterior.
Cuboid & 3 cuneiforms — the distal row articulating with the metatarsals.

Metatarsals 1–5 (the 1st is short & stout for weight-bearing); the great toe has 2 phalanges, each other toe has 3.

Ossification — Clinically Useful Points
The hip bone ossifies from three primary centres that fuse at the acetabulum through the triradiate cartilage (fuses ~15–16 yr, complete ~20–25 yr).
The distal femoral epiphysis is present at birth — a medico-legal marker of a full-term fetus.
The calcaneus is the only tarsal with a secondary (apophyseal) centre — the site of Sever’s disease (calcaneal apophysitis) in children.
Long bones grow at epiphyseal (growth) plates; physeal fractures in children are graded by the Salter–Harris classification.

The Hip Joint

A multiaxial ball-and-socket joint built for stability — the opposite trade-off to the shoulder.

Stability
  • The deep acetabulum is further deepened by the fibrocartilaginous labrum — it grips more than half the head
  • Strong capsule & three reinforcing ligaments make dislocation uncommon (cf. the shoulder)
  • The iliofemoral ligament (Y-shaped) is the strongest ligament in the body — it limits hyperextension
  • Pubofemoral (limits abduction/extension) & ischiofemoral (limits medial rotation) ligaments complete the sleeve
Blood supply & the fovea
  • Mostly the medial femoral circumflex artery → retinacular vessels (torn in intracapsular NOF # → AVN)
  • The artery of the ligamentum teres runs to the fovea — significant in children, minor in adults
  • Movements: flexion (iliopsoas), extension (glut max, hamstrings), abduction (glut med/min), adduction, rotation
The Knee Joint

The largest joint in the body — a modified hinge (bicondylar) combining the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral articulations. Stability comes almost entirely from ligaments & muscles, not bone.

Menisci & ligaments
  • Menisci deepen the tibial plateau & absorb shock; the medial meniscus is C-shaped, less mobile & attached to the MCL → more often torn
  • Cruciates (intracapsular): ACL resists anterior tibial draw; PCL resists posterior draw
  • Collaterals: MCL resists valgus, LCL resists varus
Locking & unlocking
  • Screw-home mechanism: in terminal extension the tibia laterally rotates on the femur, locking the knee for effortless standing
  • Popliteus unlocks it — it medially rotates the tibia (or laterally rotates the femur) to begin flexion
  • Bursae (suprapatellar, prepatellar, infrapatellar) can inflame (“housemaid’s/clergyman’s knee”)
The Ankle & Tibiofibular Joints
The mortise
  • The tibia (plafond + medial malleolus) & fibula (lateral malleolus) form a mortise that grips the talus
  • Held together by the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis — disrupted in Weber C fractures
  • Most stable in dorsiflexion — the talus is wider anteriorly and wedges into the mortise (so most sprains occur in plantarflexion)
Ligaments & the subtalar joint
  • Medial (deltoid) ligament — strong; resists eversion (severe eversion avulses the medial malleolus rather than tearing it)
  • Lateral ligament — ATFL, CFL, PTFL; resists inversion; the ATFL is the most commonly injured in an inversion sprain
  • The subtalar joint produces inversion & eversion
Arches of the Foot

Three arches distribute weight and act as a shock-absorbing spring: two longitudinal and one transverse.

Medial longitudinal arch — the highest; calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms & metatarsals 1–3.
Lateral longitudinal arch — flatter; calcaneus, cuboid & metatarsals 4–5.
Transverse arch — across the cuneiforms & metatarsal bases.
Support: bone shape + ligaments (spring [plantar calcaneonavicular], long/short plantar, plantar aponeurosis) + muscles (tibialis posterior, intrinsics).
Fallen & high arches. Pes planus (flat foot) — loss of the medial arch, often from spring-ligament / tibialis-posterior failure. Pes cavus — an abnormally high arch, sometimes neurological (e.g. Charcot–Marie–Tooth). The plantar aponeurosis is the key passive tie-beam; its inflammation is plantar fasciitis.
🧠 Mnemonics
Tarsal bones — “Tiger Cubs Need MILC” (Talus, Calcaneus, Navicular, Cuboid, Medial/Intermediate/Lateral cuneiforms).
Hip ligaments — iliofemoral (strongest, Y-shaped, limits extension), pubofemoral, ischiofemoral.
Lateral ankle ligaments — “Always Comes Back (Torn)”: ATFL, CFL, PTFL — ATFL most injured.
Joint types — hip = ball-and-socket; knee & ankle = hinge; subtalar = plane; pubic symphysis = secondary cartilaginous.
⭐ Exam Pearls
The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament in the body and limits hip hyperextension.
The hip is deep & stable (rarely dislocates); the shoulder is shallow & mobile (often dislocates) — opposite trade-offs.
Femoral neck–shaft angle ~125°; coxa vara <120°, coxa valga >135°.
Screw-home: the knee locks by lateral rotation of the tibia in extension; popliteus unlocks it.
Medial meniscus is attached to the MCL → torn more often (and together in the unhappy triad).
The ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion (wide anterior talus); sprains happen in plantarflexion + inversion → ATFL.
Deltoid (medial) ligament is strong → eversion tends to avulse the medial malleolus rather than tear it.
Talus has no muscle attachments and a retrograde blood supply → fracture risks avascular necrosis (like the scaphoid).
LOWER LIMB__Muscles & Movements:
Why this matters: like the arm, the lower limb is best learned by compartment — each shares a nerve, an action and a blood supply. If a thigh muscle is anterior, it is a knee extensor / hip flexor supplied by the femoral nerve; if it is posterior, it is a hamstring supplied by the sciatic. Learn the compartment → nerve → action logic and every muscle — and every “which nerve?” question — falls into place.
The Big Picture — Compartments & Their Nerves
CompartmentNerveOverall action
Anterior thighFemoral (L2–L4)Extend knee, flex hip
Medial thighObturator (L2–L4)Adduct hip
Posterior thighSciatic — tibial division (L4–S3)Extend hip, flex knee
Anterior legDeep fibularDorsiflex ankle, extend toes
Lateral legSuperficial fibularEvert foot
Posterior legTibialPlantarflex, invert, flex toes
The golden rule. In the thigh: anterior = femoral (extensors), medial = obturator (adductors), posterior = sciatic (flexors of the knee). In the leg: anterior = deep fibular (dorsiflexors), lateral = superficial fibular (evertors), posterior = tibial (plantarflexors). Get the six territories and you can localise any lesion.
Gluteal Region
The big movers
  • Gluteus maximus — powerful hip extensor & lateral rotator (rising, climbing, sprinting); inferior gluteal nerve
  • Gluteus medius & minimus — abduct & medially rotate the hip and stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance; superior gluteal nerve → their loss = Trendelenburg
  • Tensor fasciae latae — tenses the iliotibial tract; assists flexion/abduction; superior gluteal nerve
Deep lateral rotators
  • Piriformis, obturator internus, superior & inferior gemelli, quadratus femoris
  • Laterally rotate & steady the hip (like the rotator cuff of the hip)
  • Piriformis is the key landmark of the gluteal region — the sciatic nerve usually emerges just below it
Thigh — The Three Compartments
Anterior — femoral nerve
  • Quadriceps femoris — rectus femoris + vastus lateralis/medialis/intermedius → extend the knee (via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity)
  • Rectus femoris also flexes the hip (it crosses both joints)
  • Sartorius — the longest muscle; flexes, abducts & laterally rotates the hip + flexes the knee (“tailor’s position”)
  • Iliopsoas (iliacus, femoral n. + psoas major, L1–L3 rami) — the chief hip flexor
Medial — obturator nerve
  • Adductor longus, brevis & magnus, gracilis, obturator externus (+ pectineus) → adduct the hip
  • Adductor magnus has dual innervation — its hamstring part is supplied by the sciatic (tibial); its adductor hiatus transmits the femoral vessels to the popliteal fossa
  • Gracilis is the only adductor crossing the knee (it also flexes it)
Posterior — sciatic nerve (the hamstrings)
  • Biceps femoris (long + short head), semitendinosus, semimembranosus
  • Action: extend the hip & flex the knee; they also rotate the flexed knee
  • All arise from the ischial tuberosity (except the short head of biceps) and are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic — except the short head of biceps (common fibular division)

Leg — Anterior & Lateral Compartments
Anterior — deep fibular n. (dorsiflexors)
  • Tibialis anterior — dorsiflexion + inversion (its loss → foot drop)
  • Extensor digitorum longus — extends toes 2–5
  • Extensor hallucis longus — extends the great toe
  • Fibularis tertius — assists dorsiflexion & eversion
Lateral — superficial fibular n. (evertors)
  • Fibularis longus & brevis — evert the foot (and weakly plantarflex)
  • The fibularis longus tendon crosses the sole to the medial cuneiform / 1st metatarsal — helping support the arches
Leg — Posterior Compartment (the Calf)
Superficial — tibial n.
  • Gastrocnemius (two heads, crosses the knee & ankle) — plantarflexion + assists knee flexion
  • Soleus — powerful postural plantarflexor; its venous plexus is the calf-muscle “peripheral heart” pump
  • Plantaris — a small vestigial plantarflexor/knee flexor with a long slender tendon (ruptures in “tennis leg”)
  • Gastrocnemius + soleus = triceps surae → the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon → calcaneus
Deep — tibial n.
  • Tibialis posterior — inversion + plantarflexion; a key arch support
  • Flexor digitorum longus & flexor hallucis longus — flex the toes / push-off
  • Popliteus — unlocks the knee to start flexion
Behind the medial malleolus — “Tom, Dick ANd Harry”. Deep to the flexor retinaculum (the tarsal tunnel), front → back: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus. Compression here = tarsal tunnel syndrome.

MovementPrime moversNerve
DorsiflexionTibialis anterior, EDL, EHLDeep fibular
PlantarflexionGastrocnemius, soleus (+ deep muscles)Tibial
InversionTibialis anterior + tibialis posteriorDeep fibular / tibial

Invertors vs evertors — the memory hook. The two tibialis muscles (anterior & posterior) invert; the two fibularis (peroneus) muscles evert. “Tibialis turns the sole in; fibularis flips it out.”
Intrinsic Muscles of the Foot

Small muscles wholly within the foot — one dorsal (extensor digitorum brevis) and four plantar layers. They are mostly supplied by the medial & lateral plantar nerves (branches of the tibial nerve).

Role
  • Move the toes but, more importantly, support the arches and stabilise the foot during stance & push-off
  • The plantar layers mirror the hand: abductors, flexors, lumbricals & interossei
Nerves
  • Medial plantar nerve — the “median of the foot” (abductor hallucis, FDB, FHB, 1st lumbrical)
  • Lateral plantar nerve — the “ulnar of the foot” (all the rest)
  • Dorsum: extensor digitorum brevis (deep fibular nerve)
🧠 Mnemonics
Tarsal tunnel (behind medial malleolus) — “Tom, Dick ANd Harry”: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus.
Invert vs evert — Tibialis muscles invert; Fibularis (peroneus) muscles evert.
Hamstrings — biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus; all sciatic, all from the ischial tuberosity (bar the short head of biceps).
Compartment nerves — thigh: ant = femoral, med = obturator, post = sciatic; leg: ant = deep fibular, lat = superficial fibular, post = tibial.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Compartment tells you the nerve & action — the single most useful lower-limb shortcut.
Rectus femoris crosses two joints → it both flexes the hip and extends the knee.
Adductor magnus is dual-innervated (obturator + sciatic) and its hiatus transmits the femoral → popliteal artery.
Gluteus medius/minimus (superior gluteal n.) stabilise the pelvis — their loss gives a Trendelenburg gait.
Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal n.) is for power — rising from sitting, climbing, sprinting.
Tibialis anterior loss (deep fibular / anterior compartment) = foot drop; tibialis posterior loss weakens the arch.
Popliteus unlocks the extended (screw-home) knee to begin flexion.
Triceps surae (gastrocnemius + soleus) → Achilles tendon; soleus is the calf-muscle venous pump.
LOWER LIMB__Nerves:
Why this matters: the whole lower limb is wired by two plexuses — the lumbar (front & medial thigh) and the sacral (buttock, back of thigh, and everything below the knee). Learn each plexus as a map, follow the big terminal nerves along their course, and pair the peripheral-nerve territories with the dermatomes — then “which nerve/root is the lesion?” becomes one question.
The Lumbar & Sacral Plexuses — The Master Map
Lumbar plexus (T12–L4)
  • In the psoas major; supplies the anterior & medial thigh
  • Branches (“I, I Get Leftovers On Fridays”): Iliohypogastric, Ilioinguinal, Genitofemoral, Lateral cutaneous n. of thigh, Obturator, Femoral
  • The two big ones: femoral (L2–L4) & obturator (L2–L4)
Sacral plexus (L4–S4)
  • On the posterior pelvic wall; supplies the buttock, posterior thigh & the leg/foot
  • Branches: superior gluteal (L4–S1), inferior gluteal (L5–S2), sciatic (L4–S3), posterior cutaneous n. of thigh, pudendal (S2–S4)
  • The lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) links the two plexuses
The Major Nerves — Course, Motor & Sensory
Nerve (roots)MotorSensory

Femoral nerve (L2–L4)
  • Emerges lateral to psoas, passes under the inguinal ligament (lateral to the femoral artery, outside the femoral sheath) into the femoral triangle
  • Motor: the anterior thigh (knee extension & hip flexion)
  • Its longest sensory branch, the saphenous nerve, supplies the medial leg & foot
Obturator nerve (L2–L4)
  • Descends through the obturator canal into the medial thigh
  • Motor: the adductors (+ gracilis, obturator externus)
  • Sensory: a patch of medial thigh
Sciatic nerve (L4–S3) — the largest nerve in the body
  • Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, below piriformis, and descends the posterior thigh
  • Really two nerves in one sheath: the tibial and common fibular divisions
  • Motor in the thigh: the hamstrings + the hamstring part of adductor magnus
  • Divides into its two terminal nerves at the apex of the popliteal fossa
Tibial nerve (L4–S3)
  • Runs straight through the popliteal fossa into the posterior leg (supplies all its muscles)
  • Passes behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel) → divides into the medial & lateral plantar nerves (the foot intrinsics)
  • Sensory: the sole; the sural nerve (with a common-fibular twig) covers the posterolateral leg & lateral foot
Common fibular nerve (L4–S2)
  • Runs along the lateral popliteal border, then winds subcutaneously around the neck of the fibula — the most commonly injured nerve in the limb
  • Deep fibular → anterior compartment (dorsiflexors) + 1st web space
  • Superficial fibular → lateral compartment (evertors) + dorsum of the foot
  • Injury → foot drop

Dermatomes of the Lower Limb

A dermatome is the strip of skin supplied by a single spinal root. In the limb the numbers sweep down the front (L1→L5) and up the back (S1→S3). Learn the foot landmarks — they localise a root fast.

L1 — groin / upper thigh
L2–L3 — anterior & medial thigh
L4 — medial leg, medial malleolus, medial foot (knee jerk)
L5 — lateral leg, dorsum of foot & great toe
S1 — lateral foot, little toe, sole & heel (ankle jerk)
S2 — back of the thigh & leg
Foot landmarks (learn cold). L4 = medial foot / medial malleolus; L5 = dorsum of foot & big toe; S1 = little toe, lateral border & heel. “L4 to the floor (heel-walk = L4/5 dorsiflexion), S1 on your toes (tip-toe = S1 plantarflexion).”
Nerve vs Root Lesions & Reflexes
Reflex root values
  • Knee jerk (patellar) = L3–L4 — femoral nerve
  • Ankle jerk (Achilles) = S1–S2 — tibial nerve
  • A lost knee jerk + medial-leg numbness → an L4 problem; a lost ankle jerk + lateral-foot numbness → S1
Nerve vs root pattern
  • Peripheral nerve lesion → sharp territory of that nerve + its muscles
  • Root lesion → a dermatomal strip, a myotome crossing several nerves, and a lost reflex
  • Cause of a root lesion: a prolapsed intervertebral disc (radiculopathy)
Clinical Syndromes
Sciatica — L5 vs S1. A prolapsed disc (commonly L4/L5 or L5/S1) compresses a root, giving pain radiating down the leg. L5 → weak dorsiflexion / big-toe extension (EHL), numb dorsum of foot & great toe, normal reflexes. S1 → weak plantarflexion, numb lateral foot/sole, absent ankle jerk.
Common fibular palsy
  • Fibular neck # / tight cast / crossed legs → foot drop + numb dorsum of foot
  • The most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb
Meralgia paraesthetica
  • Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh under the inguinal ligament
  • Burning/numbness of the lateral thigh — no motor loss; assoc. obesity, tight belts, pregnancy
🧠 Mnemonics
Lumbar plexus branches — “I, I Get Leftovers On Fridays”: Iliohypogastric, Ilioinguinal, Genitofemoral, Lateral cutaneous n. of thigh, Obturator, Femoral.
Reflex roots — knee jerk L3–L4, ankle jerk S1–S2 (count up the limb: 1-2 ankle, 3-4 knee).
Foot roots — L4 medial, L5 dorsum/great toe, S1 lateral/heel.
Sciatic = tibial + common fibular, splitting at the top of the popliteal fossa; below piriformis at the gluteal region.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Femoral nerve = anterior thigh + saphenous (medial leg); it lies outside the femoral sheath, lateral to the artery.
Obturator = medial thigh adductors; sciatic = posterior thigh + all below the knee.
Sciatic exits below piriformis and splits into tibial + common fibular at the apex of the popliteal fossa.
Common fibular winds round the fibular neck → most-injured LL nerve → foot drop.
Tibial passes behind the medial malleolus → medial & lateral plantar nerves (foot intrinsics + sole).
Knee jerk L3–L4 (femoral); ankle jerk S1–S2 (tibial).
L5 sciatica → weak dorsiflexion, numb great toe, normal reflexes; S1 → weak plantarflexion, absent ankle jerk.
Meralgia paraesthetica = lateral cutaneous n. of thigh entrapment — pure sensory, burning lateral thigh.
LOWER LIMB__Vessels & Lymphatics:
Why this matters: like the arm, one artery feeds the whole limb and simply changes name at each landmark — external iliac → femoral → popliteal → the tibial arteries → the foot. Learn where each name-change happens and where each pulse is felt, add the two saphenous veins and the inguinal nodes, and both the anatomy spotter and the “this leg is ischaemic” clinical question are covered.
The Arterial Pipeline — One Vessel, Many Names
ArteryBecomes the next at…
External iliac→ femoral as it passes under the inguinal ligament (mid-inguinal point)
Femoral→ popliteal as it passes through the adductor hiatus
Popliteal→ anterior tibial + tibioperoneal trunk at the lower border of popliteus
Anterior tibial→ dorsalis pedis at the front of the ankle
Posterior tibial→ medial & lateral plantar arteries → the plantar arch
The tibioperoneal trunk. The popliteal artery ends by splitting into the anterior tibial and a short tibioperoneal (tibiofibular) trunk, which then divides into the posterior tibial & fibular (peroneal) arteries. The lateral compartment has no artery of its own — it is fed by the fibular artery.
Femoral Artery, Profunda Femoris & the Adductor Canal
Femoral artery & its deep branch
  • The continuation of the external iliac; enters the femoral triangle (pulse at the mid-inguinal point)
  • Its largest branch is the profunda femoris (deep artery of the thigh) — the main blood supply of the thigh
  • Profunda gives the medial & lateral circumflex femoral arteries (the medial supplies the femoral head) and 4 perforating arteries
Adductor (Hunter’s) canal
  • A tunnel in the mid-thigh, roofed by sartorius, carrying the femoral vessels from the triangle to the adductor hiatus
  • Contents: femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve, nerve to vastus medialis
  • At the adductor hiatus the femoral artery becomes the popliteal
Popliteal Artery & the Genicular Anastomosis
Course
  • The deepest structure in the popliteal fossa (on the joint capsule/floor) → the pulse is hard to feel
  • Gives genicular branches forming the genicular anastomosis around the knee
  • Divides at the lower border of popliteus into the anterior tibial & tibioperoneal trunk
Clinical
  • The genicular anastomosis provides collateral flow if the popliteal is slowly occluded
  • The artery is tethered (adductor hiatus / soleal arch) → at risk in knee dislocation & posterior trauma
  • Popliteal aneurysm is the commonest peripheral aneurysm (often bilateral, assoc. AAA)
Arteries of the Leg & Foot — and the Pulses
The three leg arteries
  • Anterior tibial — pierces the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment → continues onto the dorsum as the dorsalis pedis
  • Posterior tibial — down the posterior compartment, behind the medial malleolus → medial & lateral plantar arteries → plantar arch
  • Fibular (peroneal) — supplies the lateral & posterior compartments
The four pulses
  • Femoral — mid-inguinal point
  • Popliteal — deep in the fossa, knee slightly flexed
  • Posterior tibial — behind the medial malleolus
  • Dorsalis pedis — dorsum of the foot, lateral to the EHL tendon
Feeling for perfusion. In peripheral arterial disease you check the distal pulses (posterior tibial & dorsalis pedis) and measure the ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI): normal ≈ 0.9–1.2; <0.9 = PAD; <0.4 = critical ischaemia. (Falsely high >1.3 in calcified vessels, e.g. diabetes.)
Venous Drainage — Superficial & Deep

A superficial set (the saphenous veins, in the fat) and a deep set (venae comitantes with the arteries), joined by perforators whose valves point inward (superficial → deep). The calf-muscle pump drives venous return against gravity.

Great (long) saphenous vein
  • The longest vein in the body; passes anterior to the medial malleolus, up the medial leg & thigh
  • Drains at the saphenofemoral junction into the femoral vein (below & lateral to the pubic tubercle)
  • Accompanied by the saphenous nerve; used as a bypass / CABG graft & for cut-down
Small (short) saphenous vein
  • Passes behind the lateral malleolus, up the back of the calf
  • Drains at the saphenopopliteal junction into the popliteal vein
  • Accompanied by the sural nerve
Varicose veins & DVT. Varicose veins — incompetent valves (at the SFJ or perforators) → dilated tortuous superficial veins. DVT — Virchow’s triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability), usually in the calf/deep veins, risking pulmonary embolism.
Lymphatic Drainage
Inguinal nodes
  • Superficial inguinal nodes — a horizontal group (drain the lower abdominal wall, buttock, perineum, external genitalia, lower anal canal & lower vagina) and a vertical group (drain the superficial lower limb via the great saphenous vein)
  • Deep inguinal nodes — medial to the femoral vein; the highest is Cloquet’s node in the femoral canal → drain to the external iliac → para-aortic nodes
Popliteal nodes & a key pearl
  • Popliteal nodes — drain the deep structures & the lateral foot/heel (small saphenous territory) → then to the deep inguinal nodes
  • Scrotal/vulval skin → superficial inguinal nodes, but the testis → para-aortic nodes (its embryological origin) — a classic exam trap
Clinical Correlations
Intermittent claudication: cramping calf pain on walking, relieved by rest — from femoro-popliteal PAD.
Critical limb ischaemia: rest pain (worse at night, relieved by hanging the leg out of bed), ulcers, gangrene.
Acute limb ischaemia — 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paraesthesia, Paralysis, Perishingly cold.
Femoral artery access at the groin — angiography, cardiac catheterisation, arterial lines.
ABPI quantifies perfusion; Buerger’s test (pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency) screens for ischaemia.
Great saphenous vein — the go-to conduit for coronary/peripheral bypass grafts.
🧠 Mnemonics
Name-changes — external iliac →(inguinal ligament)→ femoral →(adductor hiatus)→ popliteal →(lower border popliteus)→ tibials.
Adductor canal — femoral artery & vein, saphenous nerve, nerve to vastus medialis (roof = sartorius).
Pulses — femoral (mid-inguinal), popliteal (deep), posterior tibial (behind medial malleolus), dorsalis pedis (lateral to EHL).
Lymph trap — scrotum skin → inguinal, but testis → para-aortic.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Name-changes: inguinal ligament (→femoral), adductor hiatus (→popliteal), lower border of popliteus (→tibials).
Profunda femoris is the main blood supply of the thigh; the medial circumflex femoral supplies the femoral head.
The lateral compartment of the leg has no artery of its own — it is supplied by the fibular artery.
Popliteal artery is deepest → weak pulse; at risk in knee dislocation; commonest peripheral aneurysm.
Dorsalis pedis pulse lies lateral to the EHL tendon; posterior tibial behind the medial malleolus.
Great saphenous = anterior to medial malleolus → SFJ; small saphenous = behind lateral malleolus → popliteal vein.
Cloquet’s node is the highest deep inguinal node (femoral canal); deep inguinal → external iliac → para-aortic.
Testis drains to para-aortic nodes (embryology), not the inguinal nodes — a favourite trap.
